content.headline: Three years after 7 October, Israel remembers victims as Gaza remains in crisis
content.shortHeadline: Israel marks 7 October as Gaza remains in crisis
content.standfirst: Israelis commemorated those killed and taken hostage in the Hamas-led attack of 7 October 2023. The anniversary also brought renewed attention to the continuing deaths, displacement and dire conditions in Gaza.

image.caption: A man comforts a woman at the fountain at Dizengoff Square during the anniversary.

sources.originalTitle: Israelis mourn 7 October attack victims three years after deadly Hamas raid
Israel marks three years since October 7 Hamas attack – in pictures
‘Neither war nor peace’: Palestinians in Gaza on existing amid disease, despair and ruins
Gazanere gør status efter tre års krig: ‘Et liv vi aldrig havde forestillet os’

segments.body: Families and survivors gathered at memorial sites across Israel on the third anniversary of the attack, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage. At the Nova festival site, relatives remembered the 378 people killed there. Memorials and vigils were also held abroad.

segments.title: A ceasefire without security
segments.body: The anniversary unfolded amid continuing violence and severe hardship in Gaza. The Hamas-run health ministry puts the Palestinian death toll since the war began at more than 74,200; it says more than 1,400 people have been killed since the ceasefire took effect. The Israeli military says at least seven of its soldiers have died in Gaza over that period.

Palestinians interviewed in Gaza described repeated displacement, ruined homes, scarce services and fear of further attacks. The UN reports widespread damage to buildings and people still living in tents or shelters. Israel says adequate supplies are entering the territory; aid workers and UN officials cited in the reporting describe health and humanitarian needs as critical.

perspectives.body: An international aid worker described the ceasefire as one that “just isn’t a ceasefire”, citing continuing attacks and malnutrition. Israel denies shortages and says more than 600 trucks enter Gaza each day.

content.headline: Russian strikes kill 20 in one Ukrainian apartment building
content.shortHeadline: Russian attack kills 20 in Ukrainian apartment block
content.standfirst: A missile destroyed parts of a residential building in Pryluky, killing 20 people, including five children, as part of a wider wave of Russian strikes that Ukrainian officials say killed 28.

image.caption: Rescuers work at the site of a Russian attack on a residential building in Pryluky.

sources.originalTitle: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy condemns ‘vile’ attacks from Russia that killed 20 in one apartment

segments.body: The heaviest losses were in Pryluky, in the northern Chernihiv region, where a Russian missile hit a five-storey apartment building. Officials said 20 people, including five children, were killed and about 55 wounded. Rescuers searched the rubble and brought 15 survivors out of the damaged building.

segments.title: Wider attacks
segments.body: Ukraine’s interior minister put the overall death toll from the latest wave of missiles and drones at 28. Two people were also killed by falling drone debris in a suburb of Kyiv, prosecutors said. Russia’s defence ministry said its forces struck a vessel carrying military cargo to Odesa and port infrastructure, without giving further details.

content.headline: Russia and WHO give differing accounts after lab worker’s suspected plague death
content.shortHeadline: WHO seeks answers after suspected plague death in Russia
content.standfirst: A 28-year-old worker at a Siberian anti-plague institute died after developing pneumonia, but Russia has not confirmed plague as the cause. The WHO says it lacks enough information to assess the risk fully.

image.caption: WHO Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus called for clarification from Russia.

sources.originalTitle: Trump to speak to Putin about plague lab worker's death in Russia
WHO says it does not have ‘full picture’ from Russia following suspected plague death
Russian lab worker dies of suspected plague. This is what you should know
WHO og USA kræver svar efter muligt nyt pesttilfælde på russisk laboratorium

segments.body: Darya Shipilova died after falling ill while working at an anti-plague research institute in Irkutsk. Russian authorities say she died of pneumonia of unknown cause and deny that tests connected her illness to her work. Reports that she may have contracted pneumonic plague remain unconfirmed.

segments.title: Unanswered questions
segments.body: The WHO says it does not yet know how Shipilova became infected or what caused her illness, and has asked Russia to clarify conflicting reports, including an unconfirmed account of a second employee with pneumonia. The Guardian also reported quarantine restrictions at the institute and nearby hospitals; Shipilova’s mother disputed the theory that a broken test tube infected her.

perspectives.body: WHO Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said the agency could not conduct a full risk assessment without timely, complete and transparent information from Russia.

segments.title: Risk remains unclear
segments.body: Russian officials say there is no epidemic risk, while accounts of the cause and extent of exposure differ. The i Paper’s experts said the risk to the wider UK public was very low and that antibiotics can treat plague; that does not resolve what happened at the laboratory or whether anyone else was exposed.

content.headline: Christa Pike speaks after failed execution as court orders evidence preserved
content.shortHeadline: Christa Pike speaks after failed execution attempt
content.standfirst: Pike’s lawyers say she is conscious but seriously ill after surviving two lethal injections in Tennessee. A judge has ordered evidence from the execution attempt preserved; the state has not said whether it will try to execute her again.

image.caption: A judge ordered evidence from Christa Pike’s failed execution attempt preserved.

sources.originalTitle: Christa Pike 'angry and confused' after failed execution, lawyers say
Dommer: Alle beviser fra mislykket henrettelse skal gemmes
What could happen next in Christa Pike's case?
Texas carries out first US execution since Christa Pike's botched lethal injections

segments.body: Pike’s lawyer said she woke in hospital angry and confused after the 30 September attempt, in which she survived two injections of pentobarbital. Her lawyers say she remains critically ill, with pneumonia, a blood clot and difficulty swallowing. A Tennessee judge ordered the state to preserve items and records connected to the procedure.

segments.title: What happens next is uncertain
segments.body: Pike’s lawyers are seeking access to her and say she remains shackled to her hospital bed. Governor Bill Lee has paused executions in Tennessee for the rest of the year and ordered an independent investigation. Experts cited by the BBC say another lethal-injection attempt could face legal challenges; Pike’s medical condition and the investigation’s findings remain unresolved.

perspectives.body: A defence lawyer cited by the BBC said another attempt using the same method would face serious legal hurdles. Other possibilities, including a different method or commutation, are uncertain and would involve further legal steps.

segments.body: The failed attempt has also become part of a separate legal challenge in Texas. Jamaal Howard’s lawyers asked courts to delay his execution, arguing that the same drug was involved and that its supply might be degraded. Courts rejected the appeals and Texas executed Howard on Wednesday; his lawyers’ claims about the drug were allegations, not findings in the supplied reporting.

content.headline: Canada indefinitely pauses assisted dying expansion for mental illness
content.shortHeadline: Canada pauses assisted dying expansion indefinitely
content.standfirst: People whose sole condition is mental illness will not become eligible for medically assisted dying in March 2027 as planned. The government says there is not enough consensus; advocates say the exclusion denies equal rights.

image.caption: Justice Minister Sean Fraser announced the indefinite pause.

sources.originalTitle: Canada suspends plans to expand assisted dying to people with mental illness
Canada bremser udvidelse af aktiv dødshjælp til psykisk syge

segments.body: Justice Minister Sean Fraser said the government will introduce legislation to suspend the planned expansion indefinitely. A parliamentary panel recommended excluding people whose only condition is mental illness, citing disagreement over eligibility and the need for better access to mental-health services. The government says the Supreme Court could consider the issue in a pending case.

segments.title: Rights and safeguards in dispute
segments.body: Advocates for expansion argue that people with severe mental illness should have the same rights as those with physical conditions. Dying with Dignity called the decision profoundly disappointing. Fraser said the lack of agreement in the medical community over whether some mental illnesses are irremediable was a serious concern.

Canada legalised assisted dying for people with terminal illnesses in 2016 and expanded eligibility in 2021 to include some people whose deaths were not imminent. The new bill is also expected to allow some patients with progressive, incurable illnesses to consent in advance, with the final decision left to provinces.

content.headline: Germany’s AfD wins state parliament presidency with unexpected votes
content.shortHeadline: AfD secures state parliament presidency in Germany
content.standfirst: Alternative für Deutschland politician Tobias Rausch won the presidency of Saxony-Anhalt’s parliament. His 48 votes exceeded the expected support, prompting speculation that four came from the conservative CDU, which rejects cooperation with AfD.

image.caption: AfD’s Tobias Rausch is congratulated after being elected parliament president.

sources.originalTitle: ANALYSE AfD har taget et stort skridt nærmere magten i Tyskland

segments.body: Tobias Rausch of Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) won the presidency of the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament with 48 votes, four more than expected. AfD had 39 seats, and the small BSW party had indicated it would support him. The ballot was secret, so the identities of the additional voters are not established.

segments.title: Pressure on the party divide
segments.body: The result has renewed debate about the political “firewall” intended to keep AfD out of influence. The DR analysis says CDU members are widely suspected of supplying the extra votes, but the party’s parliamentary leader said a secret ballot made such claims speculation. AfD leaders welcomed the result as a challenge to the firewall.

The result could matter beyond the parliamentary presidency: AfD’s state candidate Ulrich Siegmund has said he wants to become minister-president in December. The reporting says it is unclear whether he can secure enough support, and the vote does not establish that CDU members will back him.

content.headline: OpenAI teen safeguards disputed after tests find failures in safety alerts
content.shortHeadline: Study says ChatGPT’s teen safety alerts can fail
content.standfirst: OpenAI says teen use is generally limited and often educational, but Common Sense Media says tests found key safeguards unreliable, including alerts to parents after self-harm conversations. The company disputes the methodology.

image.caption: Young people’s use of platforms such as ChatGPT is under increased scrutiny.

sources.originalTitle: OpenAI says teen ChatGPT use limited but research finds it an 'unacceptable risk'

segments.body: Common Sense Media tested ChatGPT accounts registered to teenagers and found that conversations about suicide, self-harm or disordered eating on newly created, parent-linked accounts did not trigger alerts to parents. It also found the chatbot did not reliably direct teens in crisis to professional help or a hotline.

segments.title: Competing assessments
segments.body: OpenAI said the average teen user spends less than 15 minutes a day on ChatGPT and that use often involves learning. It disputed the independent report’s methods, saying some tests may have taken place before parental controls were fully active. Common Sense Media called the product an unacceptable risk until safeguards are shown to work reliably.

content.headline: Alberta’s vote could start a binding independence referendum
content.shortHeadline: Alberta vote could set independence referendum in motion
content.standfirst: Voters on 19 October will choose whether Alberta should remain in Canada or proceed to a later binding independence referendum. Supporters point to the province’s oil wealth; opponents warn of transition costs, uncertainty and lost investment.

image.caption: Albertans vote on 19 October whether to advance to an independence referendum.

sources.originalTitle: What independence could mean for oil-rich Alberta's economy

segments.body: The 19 October vote is not itself a choice to leave Canada. It asks residents whether to stay or move ahead with a formal, binding referendum on independence at a later date. Polling cited by the BBC suggests about 20% to 25% plan to support moving to that next step.

segments.title: Economic claims collide
segments.body: Separatists say Alberta contributes more to federal finances than it receives and could retain more oil and gas revenue. Estimates differ sharply: the Alberta Prosperity Project projects a large annual surplus after new responsibilities, while a report commissioned by the provincial government estimates separation costs of C$50bn to C$170bn over five years. Economists warn the uncertainty itself could discourage investment.

Alberta has major oil and gas reserves and a high GDP per capita, but independence would require new institutions and negotiations over assets and debt. Premier Danielle Smith opposes independence; supporter Keith Wilson argues the province has the resources and leverage to succeed.

content.headline: Forever chemical detected in English rivers and groundwater, tests show
content.shortHeadline: Forever chemical found in English water tests
content.standfirst: Environment Agency testing found trifluoroacetic acid at all 50 surface-water sites and 43 of 49 groundwater sites sampled. The chemical has no UK water limit; its health effects and the scale of exposure remain under study.

image.caption: The River Ancholme had the highest TFA concentration recorded in surface water.

sources.originalTitle: Forever chemical linked to fertility issues found in rivers in England

segments.body: The Environment Agency detected trifluoroacetic acid (TFA), a persistent chemical in the PFAS group, in every surface-water sample and most groundwater samples from its initial 99 English sites tested in 2024. The highest readings were in groundwater near Finchingfield in Essex and surface water in the River Ancholme in Lincolnshire.

segments.title: Health questions remain
segments.body: The European Chemicals Agency has recommended classifying TFA as a presumed reproductive toxicant, based on animal testing; human effects are not established in the reporting. There is no UK limit for TFA in water. Two-fifths of surface-water samples exceeded the EU’s new PFAS limit for rivers and lakes if TFA were the only PFAS present.

Researchers said the levels detected do not necessarily mean health problems are occurring, but expressed concern that concentrations appear to be rising and may persist for a long time. UK drinking-water testing is under way, with results expected early next year; scientists say there is limited information on how well treatment removes TFA.

content.headline: England’s SEND reforms face rising demand and specialist staff shortages
content.shortHeadline: SEND reforms face demand and staffing pressures
content.standfirst: A thinktank warns that parents are seeking education, health and care plans before proposed reforms take effect, while councils and school groups say specialist staff shortages could limit new support. The government disputes that rollout is stalling.

image.caption: Schools minister Georgia Gould promoted the experts-at-hand scheme.

sources.originalTitle: Labour Send changes at risk as parents rush to secure support, say experts
SEND pupils’ extra support at risk with schools unable to access specialist staff

segments.body: The Institute for Government says the government’s plan to replace many education, health and care plans (EHCPs) with broader support in mainstream schools may take longer than its 2030 timetable. The report says families may be applying for EHCPs now because they are uncertain about future eligibility and support.

segments.title: Capacity to deliver
segments.body: Separately, councils and education organisations warn that shortages of educational psychologists, speech and language therapists and other specialists could undermine the “experts at hand” scheme, a key part of the reforms backed by £1.8bn over three years. Schools Week analysis cited by the i Paper found at least 36 councils had raised staffing concerns.

segments.title: Government response
segments.body: The Department for Education says the figures on increased EHCP demand are speculative and that there is no evidence proposed reforms are driving it. It says the experts scheme is being phased in over three years and that recruitment and workforce development will take time. The IfG says uncertainty over support and the pace of reform could also put spending assumptions at risk.

perspectives.body: The Department for Education says it is false to describe the rollout as stalling: local areas only began delivery last month and are expected to expand their offer over time.

content.headline: Eleven approved premises for released prisoners have closed
content.shortHeadline: Eleven prisoner hostels closed amid release pressures
content.standfirst: Seven approved premises in England and Wales closed because of staffing shortages and four because of problems including infestations or lack of running water. The closures come as thousands of prisoners are due to be released in stages.

image.caption: The dining room at Bridgewood approved premises, closed earlier this year.

sources.originalTitle: Eleven bail hostels due to house early release prisoners in England and Wales closed

segments.body: Eleven approved premises—hostels supervising people considered too dangerous for ordinary release—have closed, according to figures reported by the Guardian. Seven shut because of a lack of qualified staff; four closed over conditions including infestations or no running water. The closures amount to nearly one in eight facilities.

segments.title: Safety and capacity concerns
segments.body: Approved premises supervise about 2,000 people across England and Wales, many with complex needs. The probation inspector and the union representing probation officers warned that closures could make safe release planning harder, particularly as early releases increase pressure on accommodation.

perspectives.body: The Ministry of Justice says it is investing £700m in the Probation Service and recruiting 1,300 officers this year. It says people at risk of homelessness are offered basic accommodation and that those at highest risk will be placed in approved premises.

segments.body: About 2,000 people are scheduled to be freed in the next tranche on 13 October, with further releases planned over the following year. The ministry did not publicly identify all the closed premises; the Guardian reported that Western, Bridgewood and Lightfoot House were among them.

content.headline: Two men freed after courts replace their indefinite prison sentences
content.shortHeadline: Two prisoners freed after indefinite sentences quashed
content.standfirst: Two men who received minimum terms of two years or less as teenagers have been released after spending about two decades in custody. A court also replaced a third man’s sentence after reviewing the cases.

image.caption: Luke Ings and Liam Bennett were jailed as teenagers.

sources.originalTitle: Two men serving indefinite jail sentences freed after two decades

segments.body: A judge and magistrate quashed the indeterminate sentences of Luke Ings and Liam Bennett, who had each served about 20 years despite minimum terms of 21 and 24 months. Their replacement sentences were shorter than the time they had already spent in prison, so they were entitled to release.

segments.title: Sentencing and the wider legacy
segments.body: The court also replaced James Ward’s sentence; he had been released in 2017 after serving far beyond a one-year minimum, recalled to prison and released again in August. The Criminal Cases Review Commission referred all three cases for reconsideration. The court found there had been no proper basis for the original finding of dangerousness in Bennett’s case.

Indeterminate sentences for public protection were abolished in 2012 but not retrospectively. More than 2,000 people remain imprisoned under IPP sentences, 99% beyond their original minimum terms, according to the report. The government has said it plans legislation to end the sentences by the end of the current parliament.

content.headline: Gene therapy restores some sight in trial involving people with inherited eye-d\
content.shortHeadline: Gene therapy restores some vision in small trial
content.standfirst: Six of 10 people with advanced retinitis pigmentosa showed meaningful improvements in light sensitivity after an experimental treatment. Researchers call the results promising but say the approach cannot yet restore detailed central vision.

image.caption: The optogenetic approach aims to restore some vision using light-sensitive cells.

sources.originalTitle: Gene therapy can partly restore sight in blind people, researchers reveal

segments.body: The treatment makes surviving retinal cells sensitive to light through a single injection of genetic instructions, then uses special goggles to translate images into light pulses. In a trial of 10 people, six had clinically meaningful gains in light sensitivity; some could locate objects or follow a line while wearing the goggles.

segments.title: Early results, important limits
segments.body: The study followed participants for up to five years and reported one severe eye-related side effect, which resolved within minutes. The therapy produced monochrome perception rather than normal sight, and participants could detect objects but not faces. The researchers say their next goal is to work towards higher-resolution vision.

All participants had advanced retinitis pigmentosa. The method targets surviving retinal cells and does not depend on the precise genetic cause of sight loss, but the trial is small. An Oxford visual-neuroscience professor not involved in the work welcomed the safety findings and described the gains as important early steps.

content.headline: Paramount-Warner merger creates a major new UK television group
content.shortHeadline: Paramount-Warner merger reshapes UK television market
content.standfirst: The combined company brings Channel 5, CNN and dozens of other channels under one owner, making it the UK’s third-largest linear broadcaster by viewing share. Concerns remain over competition, news independence and planned cost savings.

image.caption: Warner Bros and Paramount are now part of the same company.

sources.originalTitle: The world has a new media giant and it wants more hobbits and Harry Potter

segments.body: Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros Discovery have completed a $110bn merger, combining a large film and television library with more than 50 UK linear channels, including Channel 5, CNN, TNT Sports and Cartoon Network. UK government analysis puts the combined viewing share at 12%, ahead of Sky and Channel 4.

segments.title: Questions over influence
segments.body: The Department for Culture, Media and Sport had raised concerns about concentration in children’s programming and international news. The UK approved the deal in August subject to conditions, including that Channel 5 remain a free-to-air public broadcaster until at least 2034 and its news arm remain editorially independent from CBS and CNN during that period.

David Ellison, the new company’s chief executive, has promised investment in content and journalism, but has not made firm long-term promises about CNN. The company is targeting at least $6bn in “synergies”, raising the prospect of cuts; a media analyst cited in the report also warned that streaming prices could rise.

content.headline: London Stock Exchange chief calls for incentives to keep UK firms listed
content.shortHeadline: LSE chief urges incentives to keep firms in Britain
content.standfirst: Dame Julia Hoggett says the UK needs to make investment in domestic shares more attractive as companies leave or look overseas to list. She backs scrapping the 0.5% share-purchase tax; the government has not said whether reform will feature in its Budget.

image.caption: Dame Julia Hoggett says negative sentiment has contributed to firms leaving the UK market.

sources.originalTitle: 'Stop throwing shade' - the woman trying to stop firms leaving the UK

segments.body: The London Stock Exchange’s chief executive says the government should offer stronger incentives for British people to invest in UK-listed companies. She argues that negative sentiment about the market and a lack of domestic investment contribute to firms choosing other exchanges or leaving London.

segments.title: Fewer new listings
segments.body: The report says 23 initial public offerings raised £2.1bn in London last year, compared with 354 in the US raising $44bn. Hoggett wants the government to abolish the 0.5% tax on purchases of UK shares and supports tax credits for domestic investors. The Confederation of British Industry has also called for lighter regulation and investor incentives.

The government declined to say whether reforms would be included in the Budget, saying tax decisions are for the chancellor to announce at fiscal events. The LSE’s main market has about 930 companies and a total value of roughly £4.9tn, but several prominent firms have moved, delisted or been acquired.

content.headline: New nursery guidance would restrict staff phone use and children’s photos
content.shortHeadline: Nursery guidance to curb staff phones and photos
content.standfirst: Government guidance expected this month would tell nursery staff and childminders not to use personal devices in childcare areas, limit routine photos and strengthen checks on work devices. The plans follow abuse and data-security cases.

image.caption: The proposed guidance would restrict digital devices in childcare settings.

sources.originalTitle: Nursery staff to be banned from using phones after ‘chilling’ child abuse case

segments.body: Under the proposed guidance, staff, childminders and visitors would be told not to use personal phones or digital devices in childcare areas. Nurseries would use designated work devices, and staff would generally take no more than one photograph of each child a day, with parents able to request extra pictures during settling-in.

segments.title: Safeguarding and privacy
segments.body: The guidance is expected to require written parental permission for photos, explain how images are stored and deleted, and call for monthly checks of work devices for suspicious activity. It would also advise against posting identifiable images on social media or uploading them to AI tools that may retain or share data.

The proposed changes follow the case of Vincent Chan, a nursery worker jailed for abusing children, and a cyberattack targeting nursery data. A union representative said staff shortages and uneven training could make safeguards harder to apply. The Department for Education says it is developing guidance to improve children’s safety when digital devices are used.

content.headline: Leak exposes 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers, authority says
content.shortHeadline: 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers exposed in data leak
content.standfirst: The figure includes people living in Denmark, people who have moved abroad and deceased citizens. The Danish Agency for Civil Protection and Preparedness advises public authorities and businesses not to rely on a CPR number as the sole way to verify identity.

image.caption: The agency recommends verifying identity by means other than CPR numbers alone.

sources.originalTitle: Det betyder cpr-læk for dig

segments.body: Nearly 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers were exposed in a major data leak, the Agency for Civil Protection and Preparedness said. The total includes current residents, people who have moved abroad and deceased people; it is not a count of 8.8 million living residents.

The agency recommends that public authorities and businesses use other ways to confirm people’s identities rather than treating a CPR number as sufficient on its own. The supplied report does not identify the leak’s cause or explain what additional protections individuals should take.

content.headline: 18,000 families who received food aid may lose home-student grants
content.shortHeadline: 18,000 food-check families may lose student grants
content.standfirst: An estimate from thinktank CEPOS finds that about 18,000 families who received a food-price payment may also lose monthly grants for children living at home under the government’s proposed SU changes. The overlap has prompted criticism from both left and right.

image.caption: Ministers presented the food-check payment that some families received.

sources.originalTitle: Nye tal: 18.000 "økonomisk trængte familier" står til at miste SU til deres børn

segments.body: The government proposes ending SU grants for 81,000 students living at home whose parents together earn more than 710,000 kroner. CEPOS estimates that around a quarter—about 18,000—are in families that recently received a food check intended for households considered financially pressured.

segments.title: Dispute over who needs support
segments.body: Liberal Alliance leader Alex Vanopslagh and Enhedslisten education spokesperson Leila Stockmarr criticised what they described as inconsistent decisions: a one-off food payment for some families, followed by the removal of a recurring student grant. Vanopslagh said his party supports ending the grant but questioned the government’s approach.

The government has defended the proposed change, with Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen saying she supports young people having jobs alongside study. The CEPOS figure is an estimate of overlap between two policies, not a government count of affected households.

content.headline: Kosovo prison plan under scrutiny after trainees charged over alleged assault
content.shortHeadline: Kosovo prison plan questioned after trainee officers charged
content.standfirst: Two Kosovo prison officers training in Denmark have been charged over an alleged assault on an inmate at Vestre Prison. The case has renewed questions about Denmark’s plan to lease prison places in Kosovo, due to open no earlier than late 2027.

image.caption: The prison in Kosovo where Denmark plans to lease 300 places.

sources.originalTitle: Fængselsbetjente fra Kosovo under oplæring sigtet for at slå indsat i Vestre Fængsel
Organisation advarede om fængselsaftale med Kosovo: ’Jeg er bestemt ikke tryg’

segments.body: The two officers are accused of jointly punching an inmate in the face and body while on duty at Vestre Prison on 5 October. Both deny the charges. Denmark’s prisons authority says it reported the incident and will review the officers’ training and work placement.

segments.title: Dispute over safeguards
segments.body: Under the agreement, Denmark plans to lease 300 places at a prison in Gjilan for foreign nationals ordered deported from Denmark. Dignity, the Danish Institute Against Torture, says the case raises concern about the treatment of inmates in Kosovo and cites earlier Council of Europe findings of credible allegations of abuse in prisons there.

perspectives.body: Dignity’s legal director said six months of training in Denmark cannot guarantee that officers will follow Danish standards once the Kosovo facility opens. The prisons authority’s director said she remained confident in cooperation with Kosovo’s authorities and would review oversight.

segments.body: The facility has been delayed and is not expected to open before late 2027 or early 2028. The agreement requires conditions and rights to correspond broadly to those in Danish prisons, but the training incident has sharpened questions about how compliance will be monitored.

content.headline: Former Danish prison officer describes violence and PTSD in an overcrowded jail
content.shortHeadline: Former officer describes prison violence and PTSD
content.standfirst: Kim Knudsen says his work in a high-security unit left him with PTSD and describes abuse of prisoners and threats against staff. Denmark’s prisons director says the account is new to her and describes it as extremely serious.

image.caption: The report examines the psychological pressures on prison officers and inmates.

sources.originalTitle: Tidligere fængselsbetjent afslører gensidig voldelig kultur

segments.body: Knudsen, who spent 20 years in a high-security prison unit, says violence and threats were part of the job and that he could no longer work full-time. He describes being scalded, stabbed by a colleague and threatened outside prison, including an incident involving his children.

segments.title: Accounts and conditions disputed
segments.body: Knudsen’s forthcoming book alleges that guards beat inmates, coordinated accounts and lied in use-of-force reports. Danmarks Fængsler director Ina Eliasen said she had not heard of this account before and that such allegations are extremely serious. She said management acts when it learns of similar cases, including reporting staff to police.

perspectives.body: Eliasen said the account had made a strong impression on her and expressed regret that staff had become ill through their work. Psychologist Rikke Høgsted said sustained threats can push staff into a survival response that impairs professional judgement.

segments.body: The Prison Officers’ Association says Denmark has a record number of inmates and historically few officers: 4,650 people for 4,300 places, with bunk beds being used in single rooms. A 2020 study found 13.5% of Danish prison officers had PTSD; the report does not establish how many current staff are affected.

content.headline: One in four Danish pupils now taught outside mainstream public schools
content.shortHeadline: One in four pupils now outside mainstream public schools
content.standfirst: A new analysis finds that the share of pupils taught outside the mainstream folkeskole has risen from one in five in 2011 to one in four, through growth in both private schooling and special-school provision.

image.caption: The share of pupils outside mainstream public schools differs widely by municipality.

source.credit: Foto: Mads Claus Rasmussen / Ritzau Scanpix

sources.originalTitle: Hver fjerde elev undervises udenfor folkeskolen

segments.body: The analysis, based on Statistics Denmark register data, finds that one in four pupils now attend private or independent schools or special schools, compared with one in five in 2011. The share varies widely by municipality, from 6% in Dragør to 45% on Bornholm.

segments.title: A widening divide?
segments.body: The analyst says the shift includes more pupils in private and independent schools as well as more pupils needing special education. School researcher Andreas Rasch-Christensen warns that, if the trend continues, it could point to a divide between private schools serving more resourceful families and mainstream public schools serving less resourceful families.

Some private-school growth reflects the closure of local public schools, but the analysis says most of the increase occurred where a public school was also nearby. The researchers do not claim that all families are leaving for the same reasons or that the trend alone proves a social divide.

content.headline: Outlying Danish municipalities lose working-age residents and tax base
content.shortHeadline: Outlying municipalities struggle to retain working-age residents
content.standfirst: Experts say migration towards larger cities and their suburbs is widening the gap in local tax bases and budgets. Lemvig is promoting itself to newcomers as its working-age population shrinks.

image.caption: Outlying municipalities face budget pressure as working-age residents move elsewhere.

sources.originalTitle: Hvor vil du helst bo? Svaret på det spørgsmål er vigtigere, end du tror - og ikke kun for dig selv

segments.body: Lemvig is among the municipalities outside the island communities with the steepest recent decline in residents of working age. Mayor Jens Lønberg says the area has relatively high earnings among workers but too few people in that age group to sustain the local tax base without equalisation payments.

segments.title: A self-reinforcing pattern
segments.body: Experts say young people’s movement to larger cities, falling birth rates and an ageing population are widening differences between municipalities. Høje-Taastrup, near Copenhagen, has gained working-age residents and higher incomes, while more remote municipalities face pressure on services and budgets.

Lønberg says more local jobs would help people who study elsewhere return home. He welcomed a government announcement aimed at reducing rules that can hinder rural development, but said it was an initial step rather than a reason to celebrate.

content.headline: Mother challenges council’s use of Instagram in support decision for ill child
content.shortHeadline: Mother disputes council’s use of Instagram in care-support decision
content.standfirst: Kolding Municipality says the mother’s growing Instagram following and small business are relevant to a review of compensation for time spent caring for her seriously ill daughter. The family disputes that reasoning and has appealed.

sources.originalTitle: Mors Instagram er skyld i manglende støtte til pasning af sygt barn, skriver kommune

segments.body: Sofie Bregnhøj Suhr says the municipality cited her Instagram growth and hobby business when changing compensation for lost earnings while she cares for Molly, who has a rare skull condition. She says her account was already growing before the family appeared in a documentary and does not show that she can return to full-time work.

segments.title: Different accounts of the evidence
segments.body: The family’s lawyer says the allowance is intended to compensate for work a parent cannot do because of a child’s disability. Kolding Municipality declined to discuss the individual case but said authorities must respond when new information may affect benefits already granted, and that complex cases are reviewed when appealed.

perspectives.body: The mother says her affiliate-link business earns about 3,000 kroner a month on average and has not grown with her follower count. The municipality says it considered that activity alongside other information in reassessing the support.

segments.body: The family has appealed to the Danish Appeals Board. The supplied report does not include a decision on the appeal or an independent assessment of the family’s care needs.

content.headline: Former German intelligence chief arrested over alleged spying and secret files
content.shortHeadline: Former German spy chief arrested over alleged espionage
content.standfirst: August Hanning is accused of obtaining about 2,000 confidential intelligence documents and sharing information with a foreign intelligence service. A separate German inquiry into a failed child abduction in Gråsten led investigators to his home, but no charge in that case is reported.

image.caption: August Hanning led Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service from 1998 to 2005.

sources.originalTitle: Mislykket bortførsel i Danmark afslørede stor spionskandale

segments.body: German prosecutors say the former head of the Federal Intelligence Service, who led the agency from 1998 to 2005, paid a former chief of staff for confidential documents and intended to use them in private consultancy work. The documents reportedly included material on Iran’s nuclear programme and the Russian military. Hanning has been remanded in custody; the reporting does not identify the alleged recipient state.

segments.title: A separate Danish connection
segments.body: The investigation began after German authorities searched Hanning’s home in 2025 during a separate inquiry into a failed attempt to abduct children in Gråsten, Denmark, in 2022. Hanning had led the security company involved. Danish police released the six guards arrested at the time and later dropped the case for lack of evidence; no charge against Hanning in that matter is reported.

German authorities have ruled out Russian involvement in the espionage investigation, while a German media report pointed to a possible connection with Azerbaijan. Prosecutors have not confirmed that account. Hanning remains accused, not convicted.

content.headline: Guardiola set to return to City as questions remain over European place
content.shortHeadline: Guardiola to return as City’s European place faces questions
content.standfirst: Pep Guardiola is expected at Manchester City’s first home match since the Premier League verdict. Separately, senior football figures are concerned City could qualify for the Champions League even if relegated.

image.caption: Manchester City won the Champions League in 2023 with a 1-0 win over Inter Milan.

sources.originalTitle: Guardiola set to attend Man City v PSG next week
Senior figures worried about Man City being in next season's Champions League

segments.body: Pep Guardiola is expected to attend Manchester City’s Champions League match against Paris St-Germain next week, his first return to the Etihad since leaving at the end of last season. It will be the club’s first home game since an independent commission found it guilty of most of the Premier League’s 115 charges.

segments.title: European qualification remains unresolved
segments.body: City deny wrongdoing and have appealed. BBC Sport reports that senior figures are concerned the club could play in the Champions League next season even if relegated: there is no automatic mechanism to remove a team that qualifies on sporting merit. The appeal and any sanction remain outstanding.

content.headline: Eckert can remain Southampton manager after suspended Spygate ban
content.shortHeadline: Eckert free to stay as Southampton boss after suspended ban
content.standfirst: The FA has given Tonda Eckert a six-week ban for his role in Southampton’s spying on opponents, but suspended it until the end of next season. The club had already been expelled from the play-offs and deducted four points.

image.caption: Tonda Eckert speaking to BBC Sport in September, days before the hearing.

sources.originalTitle: Eckert free to stay as Southampton boss as Spygate ban suspended

segments.body: Southampton manager Tonda Eckert can continue in his job after an FA commission imposed a six-week ban from all football activity but suspended it until the end of next season. He was also fined £28,000 and reprimanded. The FA has yet to say whether it will appeal.

segments.title: What the commission found
segments.body: The commission sanctioned Eckert for three breaches of FA rules. It accepted that he was not aware the actions were against EFL rules or morally wrong, and cited his contrition as significant mitigation. Southampton had admitted spying on Oxford, Ipswich and Middlesbrough; the EFL had expelled the club from the play-offs and imposed a four-point deduction.

content.headline: Rahm moves towards LIV Golf exit as league tries to secure its future
content.shortHeadline: Rahm moves towards LIV exit amid league’s uncertain future
content.standfirst: Jon Rahm’s lawyer told a bankruptcy court that the proposed terms for LIV Golf’s next phase were unacceptable to the Spaniard. A consensual separation is being discussed, but has not been finalised.

image.caption: Jon Rahm, who joined LIV Golf in 2023 after leaving the PGA Tour.

sources.originalTitle: Rahm to leave LIV Golf over 'unacceptable' terms

segments.body: Jon Rahm will leave LIV Golf after deciding that the proposed terms for its planned 2027 season are unacceptable, his lawyer told a bankruptcy court hearing. The league and Rahm’s representatives are in advanced discussions about a consensual separation, which is hoped to be finalised by a 5 November hearing.

segments.title: A wider restructuring
segments.body: LIV filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the United States after Saudi Arabia withdrew its funding. It has secured possible financing of $300m from BC Partners Credit and extended talks with players until 25 October. Other players’ contract positions remain unresolved, with a further hearing scheduled for 14 October.

content.headline: Gauff describes draining days after racist abuse and China Open exit
content.shortHeadline: Gauff says racist abuse made China Open exit ‘draining’
content.standfirst: Coco Gauff said racist messages followed a disputed point in her China Open win over Sun Xinran. She then lost in the fourth round to Elise Mertens; the WTA says it is supporting her and seeking action against the abusive content.

image.caption: Coco Gauff, who won the China Open in 2024.

sources.originalTitle: 'Draining' few days for Gauff after online racist abuse

segments.body: Coco Gauff said she had found the previous few days “draining” after receiving racist comments and direct messages online. The abuse followed a point in her third-round win over China’s Sun Xinran: Gauff stopped play because of a flickering light, and after a video review the point was replayed.

segments.title: WTA offers support
segments.body: Gauff lost 6-3 6-3 to Elise Mertens in the next round, saying she felt flat and did not sustain her level. A WTA spokesperson said the organisation was appalled, was in contact with Gauff to offer support and was seeking action against the abusive content.

content.headline: Arteta signs new Arsenal contract through to 2030
content.shortHeadline: Arteta commits to Arsenal until 2030
content.standfirst: Mikel Arteta has extended his Arsenal contract, which was due to expire at the end of this season. The manager says the club’s success is “only the beginning” after last season’s league title.

image.caption: Mikel Arteta signs a new deal with Arsenal until 2030.

sources.originalTitle: Arteta signs new contract with champions Arsenal

segments.body: Mikel Arteta has signed a new contract with Arsenal until 2030. His previous deal was due to expire at the end of this season, and the extension could see his time in charge reach a decade after he joined in December 2019.

Arteta said the club’s journey together was “only the beginning”. He has won a Premier League title and an FA Cup with Arsenal; the club also reached the Champions League final in May. Chief executive Richard Garlick said continuity under Arteta could give Arsenal a competitive advantage.

content.headline: Messi receives Argentina farewell as Ronaldo’s Portugal future is questioned
content.shortHeadline: Messi farewelled by Argentina as Ronaldo faces Portugal rift
content.standfirst: Lionel Messi marked what the report describes as his final Argentina appearance with a goal and an emotional farewell. Cristiano Ronaldo, meanwhile, accused Portugal coach Jorge Jesus of breaking his word but said he expected to return.

image.caption: Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo, two of football’s most celebrated players.

sources.originalTitle: Two icons, a glorious farewell and a potentially bitter ending

segments.body: Lionel Messi played what the report describes as his final match for Argentina, scoring against Benin in front of a sellout crowd in Buenos Aires. He had announced his international retirement in August and told supporters he left “grateful, proud and at peace”. He will continue his club career with Inter Miami.

segments.title: Ronaldo’s dispute
segments.body: Cristiano Ronaldo accused Portugal coach Jorge Jesus of an “absolute breach of trust” after being left out of the starting side, then apologised to fans and team-mates for leaving camp. He said he expected to play for Portugal again. Portuguese journalist Jose Delgado told BBC Sport he believed the relationship had been badly damaged; that remains an attributed assessment, not a confirmed retirement.

content.headline: Everton extend unbeaten run as Manchester City win eight-goal thriller
content.shortHeadline: Everton keep unbeaten run going; City win 5-3 thriller
content.standfirst: Everton beat 10-man Ipswich to continue their unbeaten run, while Manchester City defeated Sunderland 5-3 to move three points clear, according to BBC Sport’s Premier League roundup.

sources.originalTitle: Premier League

segments.body: Everton’s unbeaten run continued with a win over 10-man Ipswich. Manchester City beat Sunderland 5-3 in an eight-goal game to go three points clear at the top of the table, according to the BBC Sport Premier League roundup.

Elsewhere in the roundup, Brighton ended Arsenal’s perfect start, Leeds drew with Crystal Palace to remain unbeaten in the league, and Tottenham lost again as Aston Villa claimed their first league win. The supplied roundup does not give scores for those matches.

content.headline: Who could replace Harry Kane as England’s record-breaking striker ages?
content.shortHeadline: England weigh options for life after Kane
content.standfirst: Harry Kane has reached 91 England goals and equalled the appearance record at 125 caps, but will be 35 by Euro 2028. Thomas Tuchel says England must find different solutions rather than expect another Kane.

image.caption: Harry Kane celebrates scoring for England against Czechia.

sources.originalTitle: Do England already have their Kane replacement - or is he yet to emerge?

segments.body: Harry Kane scored twice in England’s 3-0 win over Czechia, taking his tally to 91 goals in 125 appearances and drawing level with the country’s appearance record. At 33, he remains in strong form, but he will be 35 when Euro 2028 begins.

segments.title: Different options, no like-for-like successor
segments.body: Thomas Tuchel has suggested Jude Bellingham could play as a centre-forward, but former England goalkeeper Paul Robinson argues Bellingham is better playing off another striker. Dominic Calvert-Lewin is presented as a possible deputy, while the report also considers a fluid attack without a recognised number nine and younger prospects still developing.

content.headline: Victoria Monét makes room for romance on the expansive Frequency of Love
content.shortHeadline: Victoria Monét stretches out on Frequency of Love
content.standfirst: The 22-track follow-up to Jaguar II trades some of Monét’s mischievous confidence for earnest devotion, moving between lush ballads and sounds from different eras. The ambition is compelling, though the long tracklist sometimes blurs together.

sources.originalTitle: Frequency of Love

segments.body: On Frequency of Love, Victoria Monét turns the assurance of her Jaguar albums toward love in its many forms. Swooning ballads, cinematic strings and a slow jam about prioritising pleasure sit alongside the familiar cheek of tracks such as “Head to Toe”. The overall mood is more openly romantic than her earlier work.

The review praises Monét’s range, from the contemporary groove of “Reach Out” to the midcentury echoes of “I Want You”. But across 22 tracks, a similar muted production can make some songs run together, and the guest appearances by SZA and Bruno Mars do not always bring out Monét’s strongest qualities. The album’s scope is part of its appeal and its weakness.

content.headline: Danielle Ponder turns personal upheaval into songs of grief and survival
content.shortHeadline: Danielle Ponder sings through grief and change
content.standfirst: The former public defender left law for music at 40, then faced bereavement, a miscarriage and a painful relationship. On her new album, Everything Has Changed, she turns that upheaval into songs about grief, power and learning to survive.

image.caption: Danielle Ponder, whose new album draws on grief and survival.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Men are a scam!’ The trials of Danielle Ponder, the lawyer turned singer rooting for a better world

segments.body: Danielle Ponder walked away from public-defender work in Rochester five years ago to pursue music full-time. Her debut, Some of Us Are Brave, brought critical attention and placements in television, advertising and games. But as that career gathered pace, her personal life unravelled: her brother-in-law died, her father’s dementia worsened and she had a miscarriage.

segments.title: Making space for grief
segments.body: On Everything Has Changed, the song “Blues” gives stark voice to the miscarriage and the grief that followed. Ponder says shame made it difficult to tell others what had happened; she hopes speaking plainly can help people offer one another care. The songs also reflect on a relationship she describes as a nightmare and on redirecting her energy toward friendships with women.

Ponder’s perspective is shaped by her years as a public defender, when she saw poverty treated as neglect and people imprisoned for minor offences. She connects those experiences to the themes of race and injustice in her music, while her recent videos, filmed in Dakar, express a desire to embody women’s divinity and artistic freedom.

content.headline: Liz Harris finds a restorative kind of connection beyond Grouper
content.shortHeadline: Liz Harris finds a new side of herself with Helen
content.standfirst: The solitary ambient artist’s return to the dream-pop trio Helen brought friendship and collaboration back into focus. A viral hit also exposed how easily streaming platforms can be exploited to steal independent artists’ royalties.

image.caption: Liz Harris, who records as Grouper and performs with the trio Helen.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s rational to fear the music industry’: Grouper’s Liz Harris on virality, streaming scammers and her ‘restorative’ dream-pop trio

segments.body: Liz Harris is best known for the intimate, often solitary music she makes as Grouper. On Linda’s Head, the second album from her trio Helen, she sings alongside drummer Jed Bindeman and bassist Scott Simmons. Harris says the group lets her show a brighter, more social side of herself, and that rehearsing together helped restore her spirits during medical difficulties.

segments.title: The cost of a viral hit
segments.body: During the pandemic, Grouper’s “Poison Tree” spread widely on TikTok. Harris later learned that someone else had fraudulently registered and uploaded the song, collecting an estimated six figures before she and her label were able to shut down the scam and recover what she was owed. She says fake tracks and remixes continue to make monitoring her work an exhausting task.

content.headline: The Afrobeats label risks flattening Africa’s many pop traditions
content.shortHeadline: Why one label cannot speak for African music
content.standfirst: Artists and critics argue that “Afrobeats” has become a catch-all for sounds across a vast continent. The term has helped African pop travel internationally, but can obscure local traditions and newer styles that need their own names and histories.

image.caption: Tyla, who has argued that African music should not be grouped under one label.

sources.originalTitle: The west has a blinkered view of African music – and it’s hurting the whole continent’s culture

segments.body: Tyla, Tems, Burna Boy and other artists have questioned being grouped under the Afrobeats label, which the article says is now widely applied to African pop, dance, rap, R&B, gospel and more. South African star Tyla, for example, has said she represents amapiano. The label can be useful in marketing, but it does not describe the breadth of the music.

segments.title: What gets lost
segments.body: The article traces how a term that gathered attention around contemporary West African dance music became a much broader category. It argues that this can make emerging sounds harder to document on their own terms: styles such as banku music, azonto and zanku did not gain the same lasting visibility as amapiano. Artists, media and the music industry all have a role in giving new forms context and recognition.

perspectives.body: Culture journalist Tiléwa Kazeem says international publications may treat emerging styles as too “esoteric”, while founder Dolapo Amusat argues that a sound needs documentation, lore and deliberate community-building to stand on its own.

content.headline: Haywire turn hardcore’s rough edges toward melody on I Don’t Wanna Say Goodbye
content.shortHeadline: Haywire bring a melodic edge to hardcore
content.standfirst: After a DIY tour through all 50 states helped the Boston band find a wider audience, its second album pairs hardcore’s blunt force with melodic street punk and breakup songs. The shift opens a new door without abandoning the band’s scene-minded roots.

sources.originalTitle: I Don’t Wanna Say Goodbye

segments.body: Boston band Haywire built momentum through relentless touring, improvised shows and word of mouth. Their 2025 run across all 50 states helped propel them from local venues to festival slots, a split release with Dropkick Murphys and a deal with Roadrunner. On I Don’t Wanna Say Goodbye, the band uses that attention to make a more melodic record.

The album frames a breakup through gruff vocals and catchy, often tender choruses. Songs such as “Trouble in Paradise” and “Perfect Strangers” give the band’s street-punk influences room to shine, while “Flex Your Head” keeps a sharper edge. The closing “Sincerely Yours” offers a tentative note of acceptance before the record ends abruptly, in under 20 minutes.

content.headline: Tom Morello’s first solo rock album keeps protest at the centre
content.shortHeadline: Tom Morello turns protest into a solo rock record
content.standfirst: On Everyone Gets What They Want, the Rage Against the Machine guitarist takes the microphone for his first full-length solo rock album. He discusses the political backlash, his late mother’s activism and the people he believes can still change the world.

image.caption: Tom Morello, whose new solo album continues his blend of rock and activism.

sources.originalTitle: Tom Morello on Rage Against the Machine fans turning against him

segments.body: Tom Morello describes Everyone Gets What They Want as a record for people who have “had enough”. The album combines heavy riffs with songs against racism and authoritarianism, and features Serj Tankian, Kneecap and Morello’s 15-year-old son Roman. Morello says he has never separated music from activism; to him, making art is a form of resistance.

segments.title: A family inheritance
segments.body: Morello says some older Rage Against the Machine fans have attacked his politics, including his support for Covid vaccination. He rejects the idea that the band’s message was ever about individual grievance. His own outlook, he says, came from his mother, Mary Morello, whose activism included opposing racism and supporting workers’ causes. He has established a memorial project encouraging people to act on issues she cared about.

content.headline: Marc Almond says Soft Cell’s final album brings the band’s story full circle
content.shortHeadline: Marc Almond reflects on Soft Cell’s final album
content.standfirst: Soft Cell finished Danceteria shortly before keyboardist Dave Ball died in 2025. Marc Almond recalls the duo’s early rise, their unruly New York years and the sense of closure in releasing one last record together.

image.caption: Marc Almond and Dave Ball, whose final Soft Cell album was completed shortly before Ball’s death.

sources.originalTitle: Soft Cell’s Marc Almond: ‘We finished the album – two days later Dave passed away’

segments.body: Marc Almond says he and Dave Ball agreed that the new Soft Cell songs were finished; Ball died two days later, aged 66. Almond calls Danceteria the duo’s sixth and final album, and says he would not make another Soft Cell record without his bandmate. Its songs revisit the pair’s adventures in early-1980s New York.

segments.title: A scene remembered
segments.body: Almond recalls how two art students who expected to remain an underground act were thrust into pop stardom by “Tainted Love”. New York offered an escape from the pressure to conform, but he also remembers the city’s gay nightlife becoming fearful and desolate as AIDS spread. The album’s celebration of club life is shadowed by loneliness and loss.

content.headline: The Beatles’ Rubber Soul remains a work of productive contradictions
content.shortHeadline: Rubber Soul still has no single definitive form
content.standfirst: A new deluxe edition revisits the Beatles’ pivotal 1965 album through alternate mixes, outtakes and studio history. The review finds its greatest pleasure not in settling which version is definitive, but in hearing how the record changed along the way.

sources.originalTitle: Rubber Soul (Super Deluxe)

segments.body: The new Rubber Soul special edition includes the UK and US albums, stereo and mono mixes, outtakes and a detailed account of the recording sessions. The review places the record at a turning point for both the Beatles and pop: a meeting point for folk and R&B, art and commerce, and songs that could be intimate yet speak to a generation.

The outtakes reveal a group working under deadline rather than a band inevitably arriving at a masterpiece. Differences between the original national editions, mixes and later remixes reinforce the review’s central point: there is no single “real” Rubber Soul. The new set is a lavish object, but its most rewarding effect is to make a canonical record feel human and still in flux.

content.headline: The Social Reckoning’s mixed reviews expose the limits of Hollywood’s tech scept
content.shortHeadline: The Social Reckoning stumbles over its tech reckoning
content.standfirst: Aaron Sorkin’s sequel follows a whistleblower and journalist challenging Facebook’s practices, but two reviews question its dramatic force. Its arrival alongside other films about tech leaders also raises a wider question: can studios meaningfully criticise an industry they are increasingly tied to?

image.caption: Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.

sources.originalTitle: The Social Reckoning review – Aaron Sorkin’s jittery sequel with all-new evil puppet Zuckerberg
The Social Reckoning review: Aaron Sorkin's drama puts Facebook on trial, but it won't change anyone's minds ★★☆☆☆
Will the Zuckerberg, Musk and Altman movies make a dent on tech giant evangelism?

segments.body: The Social Reckoning centres on former Facebook employee Frances Haugen and Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz as they investigate the company’s impact and its handling of political content. The Guardian’s review finds an entertaining, fast-moving drama, but argues that Mark Zuckerberg is reduced to a near-cameo and that the film avoids naming Trump while discussing the rise of extremist groups.

perspectives.body: The BBC review is more dismissive of the film’s pace and stakes: it says the whistleblower story lacks the tension of a crusading newspaper drama, and that Zuckerberg’s continued power makes a decisive reckoning feel unlikely.

segments.title: A bigger industry question
segments.body: A separate Guardian analysis places the film alongside projects about Elon Musk and Sam Altman, asking whether Hollywood’s new tech criticism signals a united front or simply follows growing public scepticism. It points to the industry’s financial ties to technology companies and warns that marketing buzz is not the same as challenging tech power.

content.headline: Eva Marie Saint, star of North by Northwest and On the Waterfront, dies at 102
content.shortHeadline: Eva Marie Saint’s screen legacy, from Hitchcock to Kazan
content.standfirst: Saint’s screen career stretched across six decades, from her Oscar-winning role in On the Waterfront to her unforgettable turn as Eve Kendall in North by Northwest. A critical appreciation traces how she brought complexity to the cool blonde persona that made her famous.

image.caption: Eva Marie Saint as Eve Kendall in North by Northwest.

sources.originalTitle: Eva Marie Saint, star of North by Northwest and On the Waterfront, dies aged 102
Eva Marie Saint: the Hitchcock Blonde who outgrew the persona

segments.body: Eva Marie Saint has died aged 102, a family spokesman said. Her screen debut was opposite Marlon Brando in On the Waterfront, for which she won the supporting-actress Oscar. She later starred opposite Cary Grant in Alfred Hitchcock’s North by Northwest and continued acting in film and television for decades, including as Martha Kent in Superman Returns.

segments.title: Beyond the Hitchcock blonde
segments.body: The Guardian’s appreciation argues that Saint’s famous role as the poised, enigmatic Eve Kendall should not obscure the range beneath the image. In North by Northwest, a brief moment of fear and tears punctures her polished appearance; in On the Waterfront and later dramas, Saint brought moral force and emotional restraint to very different characters.

perspectives.body: The appreciation stresses that Saint’s controlled Hitchcock persona was only one part of her career: her work in films such as On the Waterfront and Loving revealed a quieter, more varied subtlety.

content.headline: 24 Hour Party People still captures Tony Wilson’s Manchester world
content.shortHeadline: 24 Hour Party People remains a restless Manchester portrait
content.standfirst: Michael Winterbottom’s 2002 film about Factory Records impresario Tony Wilson returns to cinemas. Its loose, self-aware style can feel formless, but Steve Coogan’s performance suits a media figure who straddled television and the music scene.

image.caption: Steve Coogan as Tony Wilson in 24 Hour Party People.

sources.originalTitle: 24 Hour Party People review – daring metatextual paean to the Manchester music scene

segments.body: Steve Coogan plays Tony Wilson, the television journalist and Factory Records impresario who championed Manchester acts including Joy Division, New Order and Happy Mondays. The film follows Wilson’s promotion of punk and post-punk, his unusual approach to contracts and the eventual collapse of Factory’s business.

The review finds the film’s fourth-wall breaks, real-world cameos and documentary-like touches especially apt for Wilson, a broadcaster who also shaped events beyond the camera. Its baggy, detached energy can make the story feel formless, but the film remains an absorbing, unusual portrait of a music scene and its self-mythologising guide.

content.headline: Artificial turns Sam Altman’s OpenAI story into an uneven tech satire
content.shortHeadline: Artificial’s tech satire is sharp but muddled
content.standfirst: Luca Guadagnino’s film casts Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman and revisits OpenAI’s early history as comedy and satire. The review admires Garfield’s performance but finds the film’s broad jokes and obvious metaphors blunt its critique.

image.caption: Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman and Yura Borisov as Ilya Sutskever in Artificial.

sources.originalTitle: Artificial review – Luca Guadagnino takes on OpenAI in muddled tech satire

segments.body: Artificial follows Ilya Sutskever’s work on artificial intelligence and his relationship with Sam Altman, played by Andrew Garfield, as OpenAI grows and its leadership tensions sharpen. The film presents Altman as self-interested and manipulative, while contrasting his ambitions with Sutskever’s belief in the technology’s promise.

The review calls Garfield’s performance sharply comic, but says the satire offers limited insight into Altman or the wider culture that welcomes tech leaders. Broad jokes and conspicuous visual metaphors interrupt the film’s more unsettling moments, leaving its warning about AI less focused than its subject demands.

content.headline: James Dean’s East of Eden performance reveals the vulnerable boy behind the icon
content.shortHeadline: The James Dean behind the rebel image
content.standfirst: A close look at East of Eden revisits Dean’s brief career and the intense working relationship with director Elia Kazan that shaped his breakthrough. The film’s most moving moment, the essay argues, is not his cool defiance but his desperate reach for a father’s affection.

image.caption: James Dean on the set of Giant in 1955.

sources.originalTitle: The truth about James Dean

segments.body: James Dean was still an unknown stage actor when Elia Kazan cast him as Cal in East of Eden. The film’s unscripted moments drew on Dean’s own strained relationship with his father, and helped create the restless, unpredictable screen presence that would become inseparable from his image.

The essay argues that the familiar rebel mythology can obscure the vulnerability in Dean’s work. It singles out a scene in which Cal, devastated by his father’s rejection of a birthday gift, reaches out to embrace him. Dean died aged 24, before he could see two of his three leading films released.

content.headline: Digger’s outsize Tom Cruise performance is lost in its own spectacle
content.shortHeadline: Digger is too big for Tom Cruise’s performance
content.standfirst: Tom Cruise plays a wealthy oil baron in prosthetics in Alejandro González Iñárritu’s new satire. The review argues that Cruise’s self-conscious performance overwhelms the film’s quieter moments and its environmental warning.

image.caption: Tom Cruise in prosthetics as the oil baron Digger Rockwell.

sources.originalTitle: Tom Cruise has forgotten how to act

segments.body: In Digger, Tom Cruise plays an ageing oil baron whose company has helped trigger an environmental catastrophe. The i review describes the role as an apparent bid for a transformative, awards-friendly performance, complete with prosthetics, a drawl and an unusually broad physical presence.

The review’s objection is not that Cruise lacks technical skill, but that his image as a meticulous global star remains too visible on screen. Even a scene meant to show private reflection feels like Cruise demonstrating his range. The film’s self-aware performance and publicity make it difficult, the critic argues, to see the character apart from the star.

content.headline: Sense and Sensibility makes Austen’s emotional balancing act feel current
content.shortHeadline: Austen’s Sense and Sensibility speaks to the present
content.standfirst: Georgia Oakley’s darker new adaptation follows sisters Elinor and Marianne as they navigate love, money and social expectations. The review finds the film uneven, but sees its central tension—between restraint and romantic impulse—as strikingly familiar.

image.caption: Daisy Edgar-Jones as Elinor Dashwood in Georgia Oakley’s Sense and Sensibility.

sources.originalTitle: Every millennial should read Sense and Sensibility

segments.body: In Georgia Oakley’s adaptation, Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles play Elinor and Marianne Dashwood, sisters with contrasting temperaments who must face financial insecurity after their family loses its fortune. The film is darker than the familiar 1995 version and, the review says, has a mixed but often compelling approach to Austen’s story.

The review connects the sisters’ different instincts to a modern pressure to balance emotional openness with self-control, and personal fulfilment with the need for security. Marianne’s attraction to Willoughby, whose intentions are “every day implied but never professedly declared”, feels especially recognisable to the critic as a modern situationship.

content.headline: Carrie’s new television adaptation divides critics over its softened heroine
content.shortHeadline: Carrie’s reinvention splits critics over its rage
content.standfirst: Mike Flanagan’s eight-part adaptation shifts Stephen King’s story into the social-media era and gives its characters more sympathetic histories. Critics disagree on whether that creates richer drama or takes the teeth out of Carrie’s revenge.

image.caption: Summer H Howell as Carrie in Mike Flanagan’s adaptation.

sources.originalTitle: Carrie review – the teenage hell-raiser’s glorious return couldn’t come at a better time
Why a new TV version of horror classic Carrie is already annoying people
Cruel torment, depraved violence, evil turns: where did TV’s real baddies go?
The Carrie remake made me furious

segments.body: The new series begins after a school fire and works backward to Carrie White’s arrival at high school. Unlike earlier versions, she has been homeschooled, and her mother and classmates are given more context than in the novel. The bullying spreads through phones and social media, while the story also spends time on the people around Carrie.

perspectives.body: The i critic argues that the series removes the anger and agency that made King’s Carrie compelling, recasting her as a frightened figure while softening her mother and tormentors.

segments.title: Reinvention or defanging?
segments.body: The Guardian review welcomes the expanded character work, calling the series an intelligent coming-of-age drama as well as horror. The BBC’s advance discussion notes debate over Carrie’s appearance and her departure from the book, but says the show modernises its themes. A separate Guardian essay argues that this sympathetic approach reflects a wider trend of giving television’s villains understandable backstories.

perspectives.body: The Guardian review sees the series’ attention to Carrie’s family and classmates as a source of emotional richness, even as it makes the adaptation kinder than the original film.

content.headline: Bel honours Beldina Odenyo through the music her sister could not leave behind
content.shortHeadline: Bel keeps Beldina Odenyo’s music alive
content.standfirst: The documentary follows Leah McAleer as she tries to complete the album of her sister, the Kenyan-Scottish singer Beldina Odenyo, who died in 2021. It is also a portrait of an extraordinary voice shaped by trauma, racism and mental illness.

image.caption: Beldina Odenyo, whose music and life are the subject of the documentary Bel.

sources.originalTitle: Bel review – a tearful, heartbreaking tribute to a spellbinding singer

segments.body: Beldina Odenyo was 31 when she died, two weeks after a powerful performance at Edinburgh’s Usher Hall. In Bel, director Louise Lockwood draws on Odenyo’s songs and teenage video diaries, alongside interviews with people who knew her. Her sister Leah McAleer works to finish the music Odenyo left on her computer.

The film traces Odenyo’s childhood move from Kenya to Scotland and the racism and violence she experienced growing up. It also follows her mental-health struggles and the isolation that worsened during lockdown. McAleer calls completing the album a futile attempt to bring her sister back, but the documentary becomes a careful tribute to both Odenyo’s voice and their bond.

content.headline: Damilola: The Untold Story remembers the boy behind the national tragedy
content.shortHeadline: Damilola Taylor’s friends recall a loss that haunts them
content.standfirst: John Boyega and other childhood friends recall Damilola Taylor, who was murdered in 2000, and the fear and grief that followed. The documentary avoids true-crime spectacle to focus on the people who knew him and the memories they have carried into adulthood.

image.caption: Damilola Taylor, remembered by childhood friends in the documentary.

sources.originalTitle: Damilola: The Untold Story review – John Boyega’s trauma after losing his childhood friend is haunting

segments.body: Damilola Taylor was 10 when he was killed on his way home from a library in Peckham in 2000. This one-off documentary includes John Boyega and his sister Grace, who were among the last children to see him alive. They describe their fear and grief, while other friends remember Damilola as a cheerful newcomer to the estate.

The review praises the film for avoiding graphic reconstructions and familiar true-crime profiling. Instead, grainy home footage, stylised scenes and testimony from friends, the caretaker who found Damilola and a journalist who covered the case preserve the uncertainty and pain of memory. The documentary also resists reducing the North Peckham Estate to a stereotype.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s uncertain future leaves fans waiting for a return
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who faces an uncertain future
content.standfirst: The BBC has cancelled a planned Christmas special, and its co-production deal with Disney+ has ended without a replacement Doctor announced. Fans and former contributors reflect on the show’s history and the questions facing its next revival.

image.caption: Several actors who have played the Doctor, from Christopher Eccleston to Ncuti Gatwa.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: Since Ncuti Gatwa’s departure, Doctor Who has been without a Doctor on screen. The BBC has ended its collaboration with Disney+ and cancelled a planned Christmas special; it is seeking another company to help fund future production, but none has yet stepped forward. The BBC declined interview requests for the article.

segments.title: A changing institution
segments.body: The feature traces the programme’s earlier cancellation and 2005 revival, then examines the changing showrunners, scripts and reactions to its recent casting. Contributors say its traditions of regeneration, kindness and curiosity have helped it endure, even as viewing figures fell and Gatwa and Jodie Whittaker faced abuse. The future remains unresolved.

perspectives.body: Lifelong fan Frank Skinner says the series did not need a major streaming investment simply to tell good stories, and urges the BBC to bring it back to television.

content.headline: Bake Off’s audience-choice week gives the tent a welcome shake-up
content.shortHeadline: Bake Off gets a sharper edge from its viewers
content.standfirst: Viewers set the challenges in the series’ first audience-choice week, bringing awkward family baking, improvised technicals and a wearable showstopper. The critic sees a welcome dose of unpredictability in a format whose cosy formula has grown stale.

image.caption: Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood judge a Bake Off challenge.

sources.originalTitle: Bake Off is toughening up. Good

segments.body: For the first time, viewers rather than judges Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood set the Bake Off challenges. The bakers made cheesecake with family members, faced different technical bakes using basic ingredients and attempted wearable showstoppers. The week was not as chaotic as it might have been, but it loosened the programme’s usual rules.

The review argues that Bake Off’s gentle warmth once distinguished it from harsher reality television, but that the same cosiness now feels dated.
